newsitem.title: USA: Political turmoil over Gingrich intensifies.
newsitem.headline: Political turmoil over Gingrich intensifies.

text.p: Political turmoil over ethics charges against House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich intensified on Friday as Republicans demanded an investigation of the taping of a private Gingrich phone call and Democrats said cancellation of next week's public hearings on the affair violated House rules.

The Democrats said the House Parliamentarian had confirmed that the rules did not permit Ethics Committee Chairman Nancy Johnson, a Connecticut Republican, to scrap the schedule agreed to by the committee.

Johnson on Thursday night had announced she had cancelled the hearings, set by the ethics committee in a meeting lasting nearly 14 hours. Starting on Monday they would have set out for the first time on live television full details of the case against Republican Gingrich.

Late on Friday the two Democrats on the subcommittee that investigated Gingrich released a letter to Johnson that said: "The House Parliamentarian has confirmed to both you and us that the House rules do not permit you to cancel the agreed-upon committee schedule without agreement from the members of the committee.
"We would expect you to abide by the rules of the House as interpreted by the parliamentarian," Democrat Reps. Ben Cardin of Maryland and Nancy Pelosi of California said.

Johnson acted after Democrats, angry at being faced with a Jan. 21 deadline set by the House for a vote on the penalty to be imposed on Gingrich for ethics violations, had publicly attacked the schedule because it did not allow special counsel James Cole to complete his report on the case before Jan. 21.
Democrats said that the House was being rushed to judgment. They wanted the vote delayed, but instead Johnson merely ordered the report produced sooner.
She said the report would now be completed and made public by next Thursday and "following that, we anticipate a public hearing." It appeared the only day available would be Friday.
Johnson's move appeared to have trumped Democrats by giving them the report prior to the House vote but taking away the hearings, which were much more important to them.
"If you have to make your choice, clearly the public hearing is the more important process," Cardin told reporters.

In what amounted to a plea-bargain with the ethics committee which avoided need for a public "trial," Gingrich admitted last Dec. 21 that he had brought discredit on the House by failing to get legal advice to ensure compliance with a ban on use of tax-exempt funds for possible partisan activity and to have given false information to House investigators.

The Gingrich tape controversy erupted on Friday when The New York Times reported on a conversation between the speaker, aides and political allies last Dec. 21, the day he and the ethics committee reached agreement on the charges against him.

The newspaper said the tape was made by someone in Florida "unsympathetic to Mr. Gingrich" who overhead the call on a police scanner which picked up a cellular phone transmission. The Times said it had received a transcript of the call from "a Democratic congressman hostile to Mr. Gingrich."

The tape suggested Gingrich was consulting allies on how to mount a damage-control counterattack against the charges, despite his promise to ethics investigators not to do so as part of the agreement settling the case.
